nameStory: The 'beaked' hazelnut gets its name from the unique shape of its nut husks, which extend into a long, narrow tube that looks remarkably like a bird's beak. This distinctive feature makes it easy to distinguish from other hazelnuts, whose husks are shorter and more open. The 'beak' can be nearly as long as the nut itself, creating a charming miniature bird-like silhouette.
description: Beaked hazelnut is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall, forming dense thickets through underground runners. It's a member of the birch family and produces edible nuts enclosed in those characteristic long, tubular husks that taper to a point like a bird's beak. The shrub has a multi-stemmed, somewhat irregular growth habit and can spread to form colonies over time. You'll recognize it by its heart-shaped leaves and distinctive nuts that ripen in late summer.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The nuts are enclosed in a long, narrow husk that extends 1-2 inches beyond the nut, tapering to form a distinctive 'beak' - this is the plant's calling card and looks unmistakably like a tiny bird beak

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to oval leaves with doubly-serrated edges that feel slightly rough and papery, arranged alternately on branches - they turn golden yellow in fall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Male flowers hang in drooping yellowish catkins (like tiny sausages) in early spring before leaves emerge, while female flowers are tiny red tufts barely visible at branch tips

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms multi-stemmed shrubs 6-10 feet tall that often grow in colonies, spreading by underground runners to create dense thickets

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and gray-brown, while older stems develop a slightly shreddy texture - the bark is thin and can be easily scratched with a fingernail

habitat: Beaked hazelnut thrives in the understory of mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, preferring well-drained but moist soils. You'll often find it along forest edges, in clearings, and on slopes where it gets partial sun to light shade. It commonly grows alongside other understory shrubs like elderberry and dogwood, and does well in both acidic and neutral soils.

seasonality.spring: Male catkins elongate and release pollen in early spring before leaves emerge, creating a yellow dusting. New leaves unfurl in late spring, starting bronze-green and maturing to bright green.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with mature heart-shaped foliage, the developing nuts are visible in their distinctive beaked husks throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Nuts ripen in late summer to early fall, turning brown inside their papery beaked husks, while leaves turn golden yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branched shrub with persistent brown catkins and occasionally some leftover beaked nut husks - look for the multi-stemmed growth pattern and smooth gray bark.

funFact: Beaked hazelnuts can live for over 50 years and a single mature shrub can produce up to 25 pounds of nuts in a good year - that's enough nuts to feed dozens of squirrels and chipmunks through the winter!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with American hazelnut, but the beaked hazelnut's dramatically extended tubular husk makes identification easy - if the husk looks like a bird's beak stretching well beyond the nut, you've found a beaked hazelnut. American hazelnut husks are much shorter and more open, like a frilly collar around the nut.
contextualKnowledge: The nuts are completely edible and taste similar to store-bought hazelnuts (which are actually European hazels), but they're smaller and the shells are quite hard to crack. Native Americans traditionally harvested and stored these nuts as an important winter food source.
compareHints: Among New England's hazelnuts, beaked hazelnut is distinguished by its dramatically extended nut husks that form a long tube or 'beak.' American hazelnut has much shorter, more open husks that barely extend beyond the nut. The introduced European hazel (common hazel) also has shorter husks and tends to be a larger, more tree-like shrub, while beaked hazelnut stays more compact and shrubby.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American hazelnut differs from its cousin beaked hazelnut mainly in the nut husks - American's are shorter and more open, while beaked hazelnut's extend into a long, narrow tube beyond the nut.
Common hazel differs from our native hazelnuts by producing round nuts instead of elongated ones, and growing taller with a more upright habit.
Turkish hazel towers over its New England relatives - our native American and beaked hazelnuts are shrubs that rarely exceed 15 feet, while Turkish hazel can reach 80 feet.
